title: Primary Function
learningObjectives: Relate the museum application to the armature's structural function.
student: What is the structural purpose of the concealed armature, and why is appearance a design constraint?
instructor: The armature supports the mounted tail elements and transfers their gravity load to the exhibit mounting frame. It must remain visually unobtrusive so the support does not distract from the displayed skeleton.

title: External Loads
student: Identify the supported exhibit load and armature self-weight. State their directions and how they enter the beam model.
instructor: Both act vertically downward and are modeled as uniform loads. The assigned exhibit load is independent of section choice; steel self-weight is calculated from density, gravity, and section area, then added to the exhibit load.

title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
student: Locate the assumed fixed support and explain what translations and rotation it restrains.
instructor: The equivalent fixed support is at the pelvis-region mounting frame. In the two-dimensional beam idealization it restrains horizontal translation, vertical translation, and rotation.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace force transfer through the exhibit system.
student: Trace the load path from the tail elements through the armature and anchorage to the museum support structure and foundation. Identify the principal internal actions in the armature.
instructor: Tail elements → concealed armature → pelvis-region anchorage → primary exhibit support → foundation. The simplified armature carries transverse shear and bending moment.

title: Critical Location
student: Where do the maximum shear-force and bending-moment magnitudes occur in the idealized cantilever?
instructor: Both maximum magnitudes occur at the fixed support. The bending stress is therefore evaluated at that section.

title: Mechanical Response
student: Explain why both bending yield and elastic tip deflection must be checked, and which may govern a visually constrained exhibit.
instructor: Yield is a strength limit, while deflection is a serviceability and appearance limit. A section can remain far below yield yet deflect too much; that is the baseline outcome for Candidate A.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify parameters controlling stress and deflection.
student: Identify how L, w, E, Fy, H, B, t, and I influence the bending-stress and deflection checks.
instructor: For the uniform-load cantilever, moment varies with wL2, stress varies with Mc/I, and tip deflection varies with wL4/(EI). Section dimensions determine area, self-weight, I, and c; yield strength controls the strength margin.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Translate the application into a beam model.
gradingNotes: Do not show students the instructor reference image until after this modeling task.
student: Sketch the armature as a horizontal cantilever with fixed and free ends. Show the exhibit load and steel self-weight separately (or combine them after calculating self-weight), support reactions, coordinate, and cross-section orientation. Do not infer dimensions from the photograph.
instructor: A complete model shows a straight fixed-free beam, downward uniform exhibit and self-weight loads, a vertical fixed-end reaction and resisting moment, and the rectangular tube with H vertical for strong-axis bending.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State the assumptions defining the teaching model.
student: State the assumptions required to reduce the museum exhibit to the assigned beam model, and explain how they limit real-world applicability.
instructor: Uniform static gravity loading; straight prismatic armature; ideal fixed support; strong-axis planar bending; linear elasticity and small deflection; constant E; sharp-corner hollow-section approximation; self-weight included. Torsion, local buckling, lateral instability, joint flexibility, connection stresses, visitor impact, vibration, fatigue, construction loads, and detailed bone/cradle load paths are excluded.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
student: Outline the calculation sequence needed to compare the two candidates and make a recommendation.
instructor: For each candidate: calculate design thickness, area, and strong-axis I; calculate steel self-weight and total distributed load; solve fixed-end shear and moment; calculate bending stress, yield factor of safety, and tip deflection; check envelope, strength, and deflection; compare overall outcomes.

title: Boundary Conditions and Constraint Loads
student: Using the instructor reference idealization, identify the fixed-end constraints and unknown reaction components. Why is the horizontal reaction zero for the assigned load case?
instructor: The fixed end supplies vertical reaction V0 and reaction moment M0. A horizontal reaction is available as a constraint but equals zero because the assigned loading has no horizontal component.

title: Section Properties and Self-Weight
learningObjectives: Calculate design thickness, area, inertia, and self-weight.
student: For each candidate use t = {{armature_t_factor}}tnom. Calculate area A = BH − (B − 2t)(H − 2t), strong-axis I, steel self-weight ws = ρgA, and total load w = we + ws.
instructor: Candidate A: t = {{armature_tA_mm}} mm, A = {{armature_AA_mm2}} mm2, I = {{armature_IA_mm4}} mm4, ws = {{armature_wsA_N_m}} N/m, total w = {{armature_wA_N_m}} N/m. Candidate B: t = {{armature_tB_mm}} mm, A = {{armature_AB_mm2}} mm2, I = {{armature_IB_mm4}} mm4, ws = {{armature_wsB_N_m}} N/m, total w = {{armature_wB_N_m}} N/m.

title: Fixed-End Reactions
learningObjectives: Apply cantilever equilibrium under uniform load.
student: For each candidate calculate the vertical reaction V0 = wL and fixed-end moment magnitude M0 = wL2/2.
instructor: Candidate A: V0 = {{armature_VA_N}} N, |M0| = {{armature_MA_Nm}} N·m. Candidate B: V0 = {{armature_VB_N}} N, |M0| = {{armature_MB_Nm}} N·m.

title: Elastic Tip Deflection
student: Calculate downward free-end deflection δ = wL4/(8EI) for both candidates and compare with δallow = {{armature_delta_allow_mm}} mm.

title: Stiffness-Based Modification
student: If a candidate fails deflection, explain how increasing section height or I could improve stiffness. Include the counteracting effect of increased self-weight.
instructor: Increasing section height is generally efficient because strong-axis I grows rapidly with height, reducing deflection. Added material also increases area and self-weight, so the benefit must be evaluated using the updated total load rather than holding w fixed.

title: Bending Stress and Yield Margin
learningObjectives: Evaluate bending strength for both candidates.
student: For each candidate calculate maximum elastic flexural stress σmax = M0(H/2)/I and bending-yield factor of safety n = Fy/σmax. Compare with nreq = {{armature_n_req}}.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Integrate strength, serviceability, geometry, and limitations.
student: Compare strength, deflection, and the {{armature_H_env_mm}} × {{armature_B_env_mm}} mm concealment envelope. Recommend Candidate A or B, identify the governing criterion, and state at least two limitations of the model. Do not present the result as certification of a museum installation.
